newsitem.title: USA: Major U.S. airlines earnings surpass expectations.
newsitem.headline: Major U.S. airlines earnings surpass expectations.

text.p: U.S. airlines Tuesday reported earnings that topped Wall Street expectations as strong demand, higher air fares and controlled capacity growth offset rising fuel prices.

United Airlines, American Airlines, Continental Airlines Inc. and Northwest Airlines Corp. each beat analysts' consensus earnings estimates. Even Trans World Airlines Inc., which posted a first-quarter loss of $71.6 million, had a better-than-expected quarter.

"Overall, the strength in revenues surpassed our expectations and the Street expectations. We see the strength in demand continuing for the next quarter," said Susan Donofrio, an analyst with NatWest Securities.

The airlines' revenues surpassed expectations even though the carriers enjoyed the benefit of the lapse in the passenger excise tax for only part of the first quarter. Last year, the tax was absent for eight months.

Donofrio said she was pleasantly surprised by United's and American's strong showing and expects Delta Air Lines Inc. to continue the trend when it reports its third fiscal quarter results on Thursday.

UAL Corp., United's parent, earned a record $105 million in the first quarter, compared with a loss of $23 million, as strong demand for domestic air travel fuelled a sharp turnaround from a year-earlier loss.
UAL said its income meant earnings of 92 cents a share and came on revenue of $4.12 billion. A year earlier, UAL lost 90 cents a share on sales of $3.74 billion.
Earnings per fully distributed share soared to $1.61 from 50 cents, shattering Wall Street estimates of $1.40.
UAL's stock jumped $4 to $78.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
United said labour unrest at American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., provided a modest benefit to the company.
A contract dispute at American led to a brief pilots strike in February and the surrounding publicity sent passengers scurrying to other airlines to avoid disruptions to their travel plans.
American last week beat analysts expectations even though it said first-quarter profits fell as a result of the bitter labour dispute and higher fuel and operating costs.

"American's performance in the March quarter was surprisingly strong given the operational chaos that the pilots negotiations and mini-strike caused," Dillon Read analyst Edward Starkman said in a recent research report.
Northwest Airlines Corp. also reported a strong quarter, posting income of $64.6 million, up 21 percent from the first quarter of 1996, and sales of $2.38 billion.
A year earlier, the airline earned $53.4 million, or 41 cents a share, on revenue of $2.27 billion.

Northwest said its strong domestic demand was offset by sharply higher fuel prices and a weakening yen. Northwest, the nation's fourth-largest airline, said it expects the second quarter to be even more challenging than the first.
Its stock fell 87.5 cents to $39.125 on Nasdaq.
Despite Northwest's caution, some analysts said they may raise their second-quarter estimates to account for strong demand.

But other analysts cautioned that too much weight is being placed on Wall Street earnings estimates. The consensus forecast is often overly cautious and is viewed more as the "worst case scenario," instead of an accurate gauge of earnings potential, analysts said.
The Dow Jones transportation average jumped 49.01 points or 1.97 percent to 2,535.86, while the Dow Jones industrial average gained 173.38 points to 6,833.59.
